blocks.content: This topic brings together several forward pointers from earlier in this course, covering, in full, how real secrets should actually be handled in Terraform configuration.
1. Several Forward Pointers, Converging Here
The Sensitive Variables and Sensitive Data in State topics, covered earlier in this course, both pointed forward to this exact, dedicated topic for complete, practical guidance.
This is deliberately the first topic in the Security module, secrets are often the most immediately consequential thing to get right in any real, production configuration.
Everything covered here builds directly on state and variable mechanics already understood from earlier modules, applied specifically to real, sensitive values.
By the end of this topic, handling a real secret should feel like a deliberate, well-understood decision, not a guess.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548580330-927093114.png
blocks.alt: Several forward pointers, from earlier in this course, converging here in full

blocks.content: 2. The Core Problem
A real secret, written in plain text directly inside a configuration file, is a genuine, real risk, readable by anyone with access to that file, or to the repository holding it.
This risk exists regardless of whether the variable is marked sensitive, that argument, recall, only hides CLI output, it does not encrypt the file itself.
This core problem is what every practice in this topic exists to address, keeping real secret values out of plain, static configuration entirely.
Recognizing this problem clearly is the first, real step toward handling secrets well, rather than relying on habits that only look secure.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548582419-352208285.png
blocks.alt: A real, genuine risk, present the moment a secret is written in plain text anywhere

blocks.content: 3. Environment Variables for Secrets
Recall TF_VAR_ from the Variables module, setting a secret through a shell environment variable is a genuinely real way to avoid ever writing it to a file at all.
This fits especially well in CI/CD pipelines, covered in their own module ahead, where the CI platform's own secret store injects the value directly as an environment variable.
This is one of the most practical, real patterns available, no file to accidentally commit, no plaintext value sitting on disk longer than necessary.
This approach is worth defaulting to for CI-driven applies, and using deliberately for local, manual applies too.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548584068-283301115.png
blocks.alt: A real way to avoid ever writing a secret to a file, using the shell environment instead

blocks.content:
export TF_VAR_db_password="genuinely-not-in-any-file"
terraform apply
4. A Dedicated Secrets Manager
For real, ongoing secret storage, a dedicated secrets manager, AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault, for instance, is genuinely purpose-built, encrypted storage for exactly this job.
Unlike a .tfvars file, a real secrets manager handles encryption, access control, and often rotation, automatically, as its actual, core function.
This is genuinely the more scalable, real answer for a team managing more than a handful of sensitive values across more than one real environment.
Adopting one is a real, worthwhile investment for any team managing genuinely sensitive, production-grade infrastructure.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548585732-471183230.png
blocks.alt: Real, purpose-built, encrypted storage, doing this one job properly

5. Data Sources: Reading, Not Storing
A data source, recall from the Core Concepts module, reads a secret from that dedicated manager at apply time, rather than storing the actual value anywhere in configuration.
This is the real, concrete mechanism that connects Terraform to a secrets manager, the configuration itself never contains the real, actual secret value at all.
The secret still genuinely ends up in state, covered honestly in the next section, but it is never present in the readable, version-controlled configuration files themselves.
This distinction, config versus state, is worth holding onto clearly through the rest of this topic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548587405-301547586.png
blocks.alt: Reading a secret at apply time, never storing its real value in configuration itself

blocks.content: 6. Never Commit a .tfvars File With Secrets
blocks.text: 6. Never Commit a .tfvars File With Secrets

blocks.content: A real .tfvars file holding actual secret values should never be committed to version control, exactly the same real risk as hard-coding a secret directly in a .tf file.
If a .tfvars file genuinely must hold real secrets, keeping it entirely local, and out of the repository, is the honest, necessary baseline.
This connects directly to the general principle already covered, real secret values belong in a secrets manager, or an environment variable, not a plain file at all.
A .tfvars file is genuinely fine for non-sensitive values, region, instance size, the risk is specifically real, sensitive content.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548588981-374966790.png
blocks.alt: A real .tfvars file with secrets, never committed, .gitignore a real necessary habit

blocks.content:
# .gitignore
*.tfvars
!example.tfvars
7. The Real Limit: Secrets Still Land in State
blocks.text: 7. The Real Limit: Secrets Still Land in State

blocks.content: Even with every practice in this topic applied consistently, a secret read via a data source, or set as a resource attribute, genuinely still lands in Terraform's own state.
This is exactly the honest limitation already covered in the Sensitive Data in State topic, worth recapping directly here, in this dedicated context.
This is precisely why State Security, covered in the very next topic of this module, matters just as much as the practices covered here.
Secret management and state security are genuinely two halves of the same real, complete picture, neither is sufficient entirely on its own.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548590553-694403963.png

blocks.content: 8. A Practical Checklist
Before adding any real secret to a Terraform configuration, a short, honest checklist genuinely helps confirm it is being handled well.
Confirming the secret is not written in plain text anywhere in version control is the single most important, real check.
Confirming a secrets manager or environment variable, rather than a committed file, is the actual source is the second, equally real check.
This checklist is worth applying every single time, not just for the first, most obviously sensitive value.

["Is this secret genuinely absent from every file in version control?","Does it come from a secrets manager or environment variable, not a committed file?","Is sensitive = true set, even knowing its real, honest limits?"]

blocks.content: 9. A Real, Common Mistake
Hard-coding a real secret directly inside a .tf file, even briefly, while testing, is a genuinely common, real mistake, easy to forget to remove before committing.
This is worth treating as a real, non-negotiable rule, never write an actual secret value directly into a .tf file, not even temporarily.
A pre-commit hook that scans for likely secret patterns is a genuinely worthwhile, real safeguard against this exact, common mistake.
Catching this early, before a commit, is considerably easier than trying to fully scrub a secret from real, shared git history afterward.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548592168-739965835.png

blocks.content: 11. Rotating Secrets Without Downtime
A dedicated secrets manager genuinely supports rotating a secret's real value without requiring a full, manual Terraform apply for every rotation.
Applications reading directly from the secrets manager at runtime, rather than only through Terraform, pick up a rotated value automatically, without any real redeployment.
This is a genuinely real, practical advantage over embedding a secret's value directly into Terraform-managed configuration or user data.
Designing for this from the start avoids a real, awkward situation later, needing a full apply just to rotate one, real sensitive value.

blocks.content: 12. A Real Team Practice
Documenting exactly which secrets a configuration depends on, and where each one genuinely comes from, is a small, real habit worth adopting as a team.
This mirrors the same documentation habit already covered for provisioners and workspace decisions earlier in this course.
A short, real README section listing required secrets and their real source makes onboarding a new team member considerably smoother.
This habit also makes a later security review, covered honestly in the Least Privilege topic, considerably faster and more reliable.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Keep real secret values out of plain configuration entirely, using TF_VAR_ environment variables or a dedicated secrets manager instead.
A data source reads a secret at apply time without storing its value in configuration, though it honestly still lands in state.
Never commit a .tfvars file holding real secrets, and never hard-code one directly in a .tf file, even temporarily.
